mult-by-ten.why: Multiplying by ten shifts every digit one place left, because each place is worth ten times the one to its right. The appended zero is a consequence, not a rule — which is why the trick breaks if you try to memorise it for decimals.
traps: With decimals, 'add a zero' fails: 2.5 × 10 is 25, not 2.50. Move the point instead.

mult-area-model.why: Splitting 23 × 47 into four rectangles (20×40, 20×7, 3×40, 3×7) shows you exactly what the column method is doing under the hood. It is also the distributive law, which is the single most used rule in algebra.
traps: All four pieces must be added. Forgetting the small corner piece is the usual slip.

code.note: In algebra this same split is written ~(a+b)(c+d) = ac + ad + bc + bd~.

mult-standard.why: The column algorithm is the area model written compactly: each row is one partial product, shifted left to account for its place value. Knowing that is what lets you debug it when a line comes out wrong.
traps: The shift is not optional. When multiplying by the tens digit, the partial product must start one column left.

mult-mental-tricks.why: Fast mental multiplication is a handful of moves: double and halve, multiply by ten and adjust, use a near-round number. ×5 is ×10 then halve; ×9 is ×10 minus one copy. These are worth knowing because they make estimation instant.
traps: When you round a factor up, you must subtract the excess, and the excess is a multiple of the *other* factor.
